record.original_question: Goodman [335] conjectured that if f (z) = n=1 an z then for each n > p, we have p X 2k(n + p)! |an | ≤ |ak |. (p + k)!(p − k)!(n − p − 1)!(n2 − k2 ) k=1 If the bound is true, then it is sharp in all of the variables p, n, a1 , . . . , ap . The conjecture has been proved for large subclasses ([343], [528], [667]), but is still open in general. The simplest case, namely for all 2-valent functions, is still open; but Watson [779] has made important contributions towards proving this inequality. (A. W. Goodman)

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $p \geq 1$ be a positive integer. A function $f$ analytic in the open unit disk $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ is called $p$-valent in $\mathbb{D}$ if for every complex number $w$, the equation $f(z) = w$ has at most $p$ solutions in $\mathbb{D}$ (counted with multiplicity), and there exists some $w_0$ for which it has exactly $p$ solutions.

Suppose
$$f(z) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n z^n$$
is $p$-valent in $\mathbb{D}$. Prove or disprove the following inequality: for every integer $n > p$,
$$|a_n| \;\leq\; \sum_{k=1}^{p} \frac{2k\,(n+p)!}{(p+k)!\,(p-k)!\,(n-p-1)!\,(n^2 - k^2)}\, |a_k|.$$

Establish moreover that, when valid, the inequality is sharp in each of the parameters $p$, $n$, and $a_1, \dots, a_p$.

As a special case, settle the question for all $2$-valent functions ($p = 2$).
artifact.status_search_result: Goodman's conjecture on coefficients of p-valent functions, posed in 1948, remains open in general. It has been verified for several large subclasses (e.g., functions of the form φ(z)^p with φ univalent, and for p=2,3 in certain composition classes), but the full conjecture, including the simplest case of all 2-valent functions, is still unresolved as of recent surveys and listings of open problems.
